implementation_notes: The standard library declares the operation on each context: Optional.map evaluates its closure only for a non-nil value and re-wraps the result (func map<U>(_ transform: (Wrapped) throws -> U) rethrows -> U?), Sequence.map applies the closure to every element and returns an Array, and Result.map transforms the success value while a failure passes through unchanged. The names and shapes match the functor's, so code that only needs 'the inside' is written per context - there is no Functor protocol in the stdlib - and compactMap/flatMap cover the dropping and flattening cases. Use .lazy before the first stage when the chain should defer, and AsyncSequence.map when the context is asynchronous.
pitfalls: Optional.map with a closure that itself returns an optional produces a double optional (U??) - that flattening case is flatMap, and conflating the two is the classic Swift map error.
Sequence.map is eager and allocates an Array per stage; .lazy must come before the first stage, and any later step typed as [Element] forces the whole chain.
Result.map maps only the success channel (mapError is the other side), and a throwing closure inside Optional.map needs try/try? at the call site because the operation rethrows.

variants.name: AsyncSequence.map over an asynchronous stream
variants.implementation_notes: The asynchronous context maps with the same name: AsyncSequence.map creates an asynchronous sequence that applies the closure to each element as it is awaited and returns an AsyncMapSequence, while the throwing overload returns an AsyncThrowingMapSequence so errors travel with the sequence - Apple's documentation describes map or compactMap as creating an asynchronous sequence that maps the given closure over the elements. It replaces collect-then-map (and the buffering it implies) with per-element transformation and composes with filter/prefix/reduce on the same protocol. Consume it with for await; cancelling the surrounding task is what stops an infinite source.
pitfalls: Nothing runs until a for await/terminal: the mapped sequence is lazy and single-use, and re-iterating re-runs the asynchronous source.
The closure is async and inherits the task's cancellation and isolation: a blocking call inside it stalls the concurrency pool instead of parallelising anything.

Errors select the sequence type: a throwing closure requires the throwing overload, and an unhandled error cancels the consuming task - failure handling has to be attached where the sequence is awaited.
